node.label: Barbara H. Rosenwein
node.date_label: Negotiating Space (1999) · “Worrying about Emotions in History” (2002) · Emotional Communities in the Early Middle Ages (2006)
node.description: A medieval historian whose studies of property, immunity and power led to an influential approach to the history of emotions. ‘Worrying about Emotions in History’ (2002) revisits Lucien Febvre’s call for a history of feeling and rejects the grand narrative, associated with Norbert Elias, of a movement from unrestrained medieval emotion to modern self-control. In its place she proposes emotional communities: overlapping groups that value and express emotions in different ways. In a 2010 interview she questions William Reddy’s sharp distinction between emotional regimes and emotional refuges; Reddy’s reply allowing plural regimes stands beside her objection. Emotional Communities in the Early Middle Ages (2006) is the book-length study.
node.representative_figures_and_works: Negotiating Space (1999); “Worrying about Emotions in History” (2002); Emotional Communities in the Early Middle Ages (2006; paperback 2007 distinct); answers in Jan Plamper’s interview (2010).
node.scope_note: Rests on the atlas’s earlier accepted readings of the 2002 article (pp. 821–822, 826–828, 842–845) and the 2010 interview answers. Not re-readable here (publisher paywalls). The Stearns criticism cites pp. 824–826, outside the recorded reading, and is held.

proposed_edges.relationship: Proposes overlapping emotional communities and questions a single historical trajectory toward restraint.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Existing recorded primary reading: 2002 pp. 821–822, 826–828, 842–845; 2010 Rosenwein answers pp. 255–256. Her objection to regime/refuge remains distinct from Reddy’s pp. 240–243 plural-regime qualification.

proposed_edges.relationship: Challenges the civilizing-process narrative of a progression from medieval emotional excess toward modern restraint.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Existing bounded article reading, especially pp. 826–828 and 842–845. This is Rosenwein’s historiographical objection, not a rereading or blanket rejection of all Elias scholarship.

proposed_edges.relationship: Rosenwein returns to Febvre’s programme for studying historical emotions while reconsidering the assumptions of subsequent approaches.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Previously documented primary pp. 821–822. Historiographical framing/resource; no claim of direct personal transmission or unmodified adoption.
